title: Retro 90s vs Retro Y2K
lede: Ten years apart and constantly confused. One is bevels and primary colours; the other is chrome and gloss.
verdict: The 90s page has no gradients at all — depth comes from four-colour bevels on square boxes, navy and yellow, and links that are underlined by default. Y2K has gradients everywhere, rounded corners, white borders and a chrome finish.
brief: The 90s preview is a reconstruction of browser defaults: a navy background, yellow Times text, and borders built from outset, inset and ridge styles that produce a four-colour bevel with no gradient involved. The radius is 0 on every element, because rounded corners were not available.

Y2K is the opposite: every surface is a linear gradient running light-dark-light to suggest metal, corners run to 18 to 22px, and a 1px white border traces each panel. Nothing is beveled, because by then the depth cue had moved from the border to the fill.

cssDelta.label: Headline fill
cssDelta.b: chrome gradient clipped to the glyphs

whenA: The joke is the point — a nostalgia play, an April Fool page, a deliberately dated brand
You want the page to feel like software from a specific era, not a style applied to modern layout
The audience is old enough to recognise it and the content is short
whenB: You want retro without the hostility: Y2K is dated but still comfortable to read
The brand is music, fashion or beauty, where chrome and gloss read as playful rather than broken
You need the look to survive on a phone, which bevels largely do not
promptDelta: The words matter here: ask for outset and inset borders and Times on navy for the 90s; ask for chrome gradients, 20px radii and a 1px white hairline for Y2K. Do not ask for retro in general — a model will give you Y2K for 90s roughly half the time, because that is the more documented reference. Also pin the palette explicitly: the 90s set is four values, and any additional colour immediately reads as the wrong decade.
